analysis.one_liner: Lets vitamin and supplement makers make health claims without FDA pre-approval and keeps high-potency supplements off the drug list.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 28 bipartisan cosponsors but never got a committee vote, dying when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the food and drug law so vitamins, minerals, herbs, and similar products are legally "dietary supplements," not drugs or food additives, even at high potencies. Supplement makers could put health and disease-related claims on labels and ads based on a "reasonable scientific basis" — clinical studies, expert opinion, or even unpublished reports — without proving scientific agreement to the FDA first, and only notify the agency 30 days in advance. It would also freeze planned changes to vitamin labeling standards for two years and give supplement companies the right to sue in federal court to challenge FDA warning assertions.
analysis.who_benefits: Dietary supplement manufacturers, distributors, and retailers gain the most. They could market products with disease-related claims without FDA pre-approval, keep high-potency products out of the drug approval process entirely, and lock the FDA into a 30-day notice system backed by a court challenge right. Consumers who want broader access to supplements and health information would gain more choice, but with weaker verification of the claims behind it.

how_it_helps.text: Defines "dietary supplement" in law and says a supplement is not a drug solely because of the potency of its ingredients, keeping high-dose products out of the FDA drug approval process [S2][S3].

Allows health and disease-related claims on supplement labels and ads if they are "truthful and not misleading" and premised on a reasonable scientific basis — which can include unpublished reports or expert opinion — without requiring scientific consensus, with only 30 days advance notice to the FDA [S3].
Blocks FDA from treating a supplement as a food additive when its label says it supplements the diet, and declares all essential nutrients generally recognized as safe for supplement use [S2][S3].

Lets supplement manufacturers, distributors, or retailers go to federal court for a declaratory judgment whenever the FDA asserts a claim is false or misleading, and requires the FDA to run an independent study of the recommended daily allowances before changing vitamin labeling [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers would bear the cost of weaker verification: they could buy products marketed with disease-related claims supported by unpublished or preliminary evidence, with the FDA able to act only after the claim reaches the market. The FDA loses its main tools — drug classification for high-potency products and food-additive rules — and gains a slower, litigation-exposed enforcement path.

drawbacks.text: The bill lowers the evidence bar for disease-related claims: "reasonable scientific basis" can be unpublished reports or individual expert opinion, and neither scientific consensus nor "significant scientific agreement" is required [S3]. Consumers deciding treatments based on labels could be relying on weak or one-sided evidence.

A supplement cannot be treated as a drug solely because of potency, and is excluded from food-additive rules, so high-dose products reach the market without the pre-market safety testing that applies to drugs [S2][S3].

The FDA must act after claims hit the market, and manufacturers can immediately challenge any FDA assertion in court; the law says the agency's failure to be challenged creates no presumption its assertion is valid [S3].
Existing vitamin labeling standards would be frozen for two years while a new study runs, delaying any updated dietary guidance [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters framed this as protecting consumer access to vitamins and herbs at a time when the FDA was moving to treat high-potency supplements as drugs. The trade-off is real: the same language that keeps supplements easy to buy also lets companies make disease-related claims on the strength of unpublished or non-consensus evidence, with the burden falling on the FDA to prove a claim misleading after the fact. The bill is better designed for industry marketing than for consumer protection.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its health subcommittee, where it sat until the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993 without ever getting a markup or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Richardson introduced the bill on July 31, 1992, joined by Reps. Panetta and Orton, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1][S5].
On August 26, 1992, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment, which was the last action of record [S5].

The bill gathered 28 cosponsors, 17 Democrats and 11 Republicans, but never received a committee markup, a subcommittee vote, or floor consideration before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S1][S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the FDA temporarily kept its existing authority over high-potency supplements and health claims, and consumers kept the stronger pre-market oversight the bill would have trimmed. Supplement makers would have been the beneficiaries had it passed.

for.name: Rep. Bill Richardson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Health Choices Freedom Act of 1992 on July 31, 1992.

for.name: Reps. Leon Panetta and Bill Orton
for.what_they_did: Joined Richardson as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

for.name: 28 House cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors (17 of 267 House Democrats, 11 of 176 House Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan support.

for.name: Dietary supplement industry and health-freedom groups
for.what_they_did: Backed congressional efforts in 1992-1994 to stop FDA from reclassifying high-potency supplements as drugs; the eventual result, the 1994 Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act, closely mirrors this bill's framework.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Rep. John Dingell, D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on July 31, 1992, but never scheduled a markup or reported it out.

against.name: Subcommittee on Health and the Environment
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on August 26, 1992, and took no further recorded action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Food and Drug Administration
against.what_they_did: At the time, was moving to treat high-potency supplements as drugs or food additives — the policy this bill was written to block — and would have lost pre-market tools under it.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship split 17 Democrats to 11 Republicans, with no recorded votes on either side; the bill simply died in committee without opposition ever being tested.

industries.note: The bill hands supplement makers a legal category exempt from drug and food-additive rules, lets them make disease-related claims without FDA pre-approval, and gives them a court path to fight the agency. Consumers would bear the cost in weaker verification of the claims on the bottle.
Retailers and distributors are explicitly included in the new right to sue the FDA over claim assertions, and they benefit from freer advertising of health claims.
Drug makers would face more competition from supplements marketed with disease-related claims, but the drugs pathway itself — where they hold approved products — is untouched.
